summary: Think about the last time someone in your group said a task was “done,” and it wasn’t. Same word, different meaning. On a Moon mission, that kind of mix-up can cost a landing. Dr. Heidi Kohronen, a project manager at MPIA, proclaimed: “The largest contributor to delays are ambiguous language and false consensus.” Common Horizon is a landing-day planner for the Moon’s south pole, where the Sun stays low and Earth hides behind hills. Every team on a lander decides for itself when the Sun is “up” and when Earth is “in view,” and those choices change the answer: at Malapert, Earth is in view 83% of 2028 by one meaning and only 57% by another. Using NASA terrain data, our tool shows each team’s meaning, helps everyone agree on one, and determines which landing days still work and why. With our example teams, 10 days in October looked fine, but only 4 really work. Catching this before a date is set matters: NASA found that fixing a mistake late can cost up to 1,500 times more, and a units mix-up cost NASA the $327M Mars Climate Orbiter.
details:
Common Horizon helps a lunar mission pick a landing day that truly works for every team. It starts from a simple observation we call the Pip twist. Our guide, a small lander named Pip, stands on the real horizon of an Artemis landing site while the Sun and Earth move across the sky. At the same moment, one team says Earth is in view and another says it isn’t. Both are looking at the same sky; they just mean different things by “in view.” At the lunar south pole, where the Sun circles just above the hills and Earth rises and sets behind ridges, these small differences decide which landing days are possible. Common Horizon makes that hidden disagreement visible, helps teams agree, and shows which days survive.

Underneath is a physics and geometry model built on NASA data. We use astropy’s built-in solar system positions to find the Sun, Earth and Moon every 2 hours of 2028, then turn those positions into the Moon’s own frame using the IAU 2009 model of how the Moon spins and wobbles. For each site we build a local compass of up, east and north from its latitude and longitude, and work out the direction (azimuth) and height (elevation) of the Sun and Earth, including the small shift caused by standing on the surface rather than at the Moon’s centre. The terrain comes from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter laser altimeter (LOLA) maps at 80 m and 240 m resolution. From each site we cast 720 rays, one every half degree, out to 400 km, read the height along each ray, and find the highest angle in every direction, allowing for the curve of the Moon. We do this at three heights: the ground, a 2 m lander deck and a 10 m mast. Because the Sun is a disc and not a point, we calculate what share of it shows above the hills, using the area of a circle cut by a straight line, and we store how many degrees Earth’s centre sits above the hills. On top of this we add three real-world checks: how steep the ground is, from the terrain map; whether one of NASA’s Deep Space Network dishes in California, Spain or Australia can see the Moon; and 17 spots across a 200 m landing area, with touchdown checked every 10 minutes.

The planner then simulates each mission hour by hour in the browser. Solar power comes from the real sunlight at the deck, the battery charges and drains, heaters switch on in shadow, and every team’s needs are scheduled: landing, checkout, science tasks, data to send home and regular calls with Earth. Each need is marked as a must-have or a nice-to-have, and the schedule respects the power limit, the battery floor, daily dish time and one instrument and one radio at a time. Each landing day is run with each team’s own meanings, with the agreed meaning, and with one word agreed at a time. That shows which days only looked fine and which single word causes the most trouble, so the team knows what to talk about first. Every result comes with a reason in plain words.

For users it is four steps: pick a site and month, have each team answer three picture questions, agree on one meaning, then see the answer as a calendar. Pip guides newcomers and can read every step aloud. An expert view adds battery and schedule charts, a margin for every requirement, sensitivity charts, an every-site-by-month table and spreadsheet import and export. The app runs offline as a single file, and a demo version and a real version (which starts empty and uses only your inputs) come from the same code.

The benefit is catching a costly mix-up at the cheapest moment, before a landing date is chosen. NASA found that fixing a mistake late can cost up to 1,500 times more than fixing it early. In our Malapert example, 10 landing days in October looked fine, but only 4 really work, and moving the landing spot 200 m changes the answer again. The people we spoke to on real spacecraft projects told us these mix-ups happen on their teams too. We built it for student and small company teams sending payloads to the Moon, and as a quick check before any design review.

We checked the model against independent sources. Our terrain heights match LROC QuickMap (only discrepancy 5,040 m vs 5,042 m at Mons Mouton), our lighting results are within about 5 percentage points of a published study (Bussey et al., 2010), and our slope check reads about 12° where the IM-1 Odysseus lander tipped over in 2024. Fourteen built-in physics tests confirm things like the Sun’s yearly range, Earth’s wobble and the horizon of flat ground.

What is new is that we treat the words themselves as the problem. Most landing tools rank sites by how sunny they are, using one fixed definition. Common Horizon asks whether everyone is using the same definition, and shows what happens when they aren’t.

We built the engine in Python with astropy, numpy and tifffile, and the app in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, tested with Playwright. Our data is NASA LRO LOLA terrain, astropy’s solar system positions and the IAU 2009 Moon rotation model. Along the way we balanced keeping it simple for newcomers with full detail for engineers, used real NASA data and checked it, and showed every result with its reason. We are open about our limits: we do not yet model dust, temperature, relay satellites or boulders smaller than 80 m, and the scheduler finds a working plan rather than the best possible one.
